name: API Architecture and System Design
description: 40 mid-to-senior scenario questions on API contracts, protocol trade-offs, authorization, idempotency, rate limiting, caching, and resilience. Topic selection includes anecdotal [Amazon](https://leetcode.com/discuss/interview-experience/7311674/) and [Microsoft](https://leetcode.com/discuss/interview-experience/6114211/) candidate reports; these do not establish statistical frequency. Answers use primary standards and engineering documentation. No SQL, database optimization, or Django patterns.

questions.question: Internal services in several languages need typed contracts and bidirectional streaming. Which choice most directly fits, assuming the infrastructure supports it?
options: REST with polling because all HTTP APIs support bidirectional RPC streams automatically
GraphQL because every GraphQL query is a bidirectional stream
gRPC, with generated clients and supported streaming RPCs
REST because gRPC requires every service to use the same language
questions.answer: gRPC, with generated clients and supported streaming RPCs
questions.explanation: gRPC supports generated service contracts and streaming. Browser access and intermediary compatibility still need deliberate evaluation. [Source](https://grpc.io/docs/what-is-grpc/core-concepts/).

questions.question: GraphQL lets clients request different nested response shapes. Which controls help keep that flexibility manageable?
options: Bound query complexity, depth, or total cost
Enforce authorization for accessed objects and fields
Assume one endpoint means all queries cost roughly the same
Limit batching and expensive repeated field selections
answers: Bound query complexity, depth, or total cost
Enforce authorization for accessed objects and fields
Limit batching and expensive repeated field selections
questions.explanation: Client-controlled selection can create expensive work or expose fields. GraphQL still requires demand controls and authorization. [Source](https://graphql.org/learn/security/).

questions.question: A gRPC client receives `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` for a mutation. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The server definitely rolled back the mutation
The client’s deadline expired; the mutation’s outcome may still need reconciliation
The server never received the request
The RPC can safely be retried with a new operation identifier
questions.answer: The client’s deadline expired; the mutation’s outcome may still need reconciliation
questions.explanation: Client and server can observe different outcomes. A deadline bounds how long the client waits; it does not roll back side effects that have already occurred. [Source](https://grpc.io/docs/what-is-grpc/core-concepts/#rpc-termination).

questions.question: REST statelessness prohibits a service from storing any resource data or consulting an authorization store.
questions.explanation: Statelessness concerns request interaction context, not the absence of stored resources. Each request must provide the context needed to interpret it. [REST constraints](https://ics.uci.edu/~fielding/pubs/dissertation/rest_arch_style.htm).

questions.question: Under HTTP method semantics, which statements are correct?
options: `GET` is intended to be safe
`PUT` is idempotent by defined semantics
`POST` is universally idempotent by defined semantics
A safe request may still produce incidental logging
answers: `GET` is intended to be safe
`PUT` is idempotent by defined semantics
A safe request may still produce incidental logging
questions.explanation: Safety concerns requested changes; idempotency concerns repeated intended effects. Incidental logs do not violate safety. [Source](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html).

options: `PATCH` guarantees the second request is ignored
`PATCH` guarantees complete resource replacement
The second request must return `304`
The counter may be incremented twice
questions.answer: The counter may be incremented twice
questions.explanation: Idempotency depends on operation semantics. Repeating an increment repeats its effect unless an additional deduplication mechanism intervenes. [PATCH semantics](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5789.html).

questions.question: `DELETE` can remain idempotent when the first request returns `204` and a repeated request returns `404`.
questions.explanation: Idempotency does not require identical responses. Repeating deletion can preserve the same intended resource state. [Source](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html).

questions.question: A report needs minutes to generate. Which HTTP interaction best supports asynchronous processing?
options: Return `202` with an operation identifier and a status URL
Return `200` claiming completion before generation begins
Return `204` and require clients to infer completion from elapsed time
Keep retrying the original request internally without any deadline
questions.answer: Return `202` with an operation identifier and a status URL
questions.explanation: `202` means accepted, not completed. A status resource can expose progress and the eventual result or failure. [Source](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html).

questions.question: Two clients edit the same resource version. Which API mechanism can reject a write based on an outdated representation?
options: `If-None-Match` only on an unrelated `GET`
`Cache-Control: public` on the write
`If-Match` with the strong ETag of the version being edited
A unique tracing identifier with no precondition check
questions.answer: `If-Match` with the strong ETag of the version being edited
questions.explanation: Evaluate the version precondition atomically with the update. A failed `If-Match` normally produces `412 Precondition Failed`. [Source](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html).

questions.question: An API response enum gains a new possible value. Which compatibility concern should a senior engineer raise?
options: Response additions can never affect existing clients
Clients with exhaustive enum handling may fail on the new value
Only request changes require compatibility review
HTTP automatically maps unknown enum values to `null`
questions.answer: Clients with exhaustive enum handling may fail on the new value
questions.explanation: Additive changes can still break strict clients. Define unknown-value handling and evolution expectations as part of the contract. [Source](https://google.aip.dev/180).

questions.question: For an API with opaque pagination tokens, which statements are sound?
options: Clients should treat tokens as continuation data rather than parse their internals
Possessing a token replaces authorization on subsequent page requests
The service should define token expiry and filter consistency behavior
A token alone guarantees snapshot consistency despite concurrent changes
answers: Clients should treat tokens as continuation data rather than parse their internals
The service should define token expiry and filter consistency behavior
questions.explanation: Continuation does not grant access or inherently freeze a dataset. Reauthorize requests and document consistency and token validity. [Source](https://google.aip.dev/158).

questions.question: A web application needs user sign-in and delegated API access. Which distinction is correct?
options: OAuth access tokens always prove a user’s identity to any client
OpenID Connect replaces all resource authorization checks
An ID token is automatically an access token for every API
OpenID Connect adds authentication to OAuth; access tokens authorize access to their intended resources
questions.answer: OpenID Connect adds authentication to OAuth; access tokens authorize access to their intended resources
questions.explanation: ID tokens convey authentication to a client. APIs should require tokens intended for those APIs and enforce their authorization policies. [Source](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html).

questions.question: A public native client uses the authorization-code flow. What does PKCE primarily protect against?
options: An intercepted authorization code being redeemed without the matching verifier
Every form of cross-site scripting
An access token being readable by its bearer
An authenticated user accessing unauthorized application records
questions.answer: An intercepted authorization code being redeemed without the matching verifier
questions.explanation: PKCE binds code redemption to a verifier established by the initiating client. It does not replace other authentication or authorization defenses. [Source](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html).

questions.question: Which checks belong in validation of a JWT access token at its intended API?
options: Verify its signature using trusted keys and an allowed algorithm
Accept any algorithm named in the untrusted token header
Validate issuer, audience, and applicable time claims
Check that its token type and claims fit the expected access-token profile
answers: Verify its signature using trusted keys and an allowed algorithm
Validate issuer, audience, and applicable time claims
Check that its token type and claims fit the expected access-token profile
questions.explanation: Decoding is not validation. A valid signature alone does not establish that the token is suitable for this API or purpose. [Source](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8725.html).

questions.question: A self-contained access token remains cryptographically valid for 30 minutes, but access must be revoked immediately. What additional design is needed?
options: Deleting the browser’s token guarantees all copies stop working
Online revocation or session-state checks, accepting their availability and caching trade-offs
Base64-encoding the token again
Adding a longer expiration time to reduce replay
questions.answer: Online revocation or session-state checks, accepting their availability and caching trade-offs
questions.explanation: Offline signature checks cannot discover new revocation state. Immediate revocation requires current state at enforcement time; cached positive checks can leave a window of revoked access unless reliably invalidated before reuse. [Source](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7662.html#section-4).

questions.question: A token has `invoices.read`. The caller requests an invoice owned by another tenant. What should determine access?
options: The scope alone, because scopes identify each allowed record
Whether the caller knows the invoice identifier
Server-side tenant and resource authorization in addition to the scope
Whether the identifier is a UUID
questions.answer: Server-side tenant and resource authorization in addition to the scope
questions.explanation: A coarse permission does not authorize every matching object. Enforce tenant, ownership, and field rules at the resource boundary. [Source](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html).

questions.question: A background service uses its own client-credentials token. What identity should downstream authorization normally evaluate?
options: The last human who logged into the service
Any user identifier placed in the request body
An administrator because no human is present
The service principal and its explicitly granted permissions
questions.answer: The service principal and its explicitly granted permissions
questions.explanation: Application identity does not imply delegated user authority. Acting for a user requires a separately trusted delegation mechanism. [Client credentials](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749.html#section-4.4).

questions.question: CORS restrictions are enforced by browsers and do not prevent a non-browser HTTP client from calling an API.
questions.explanation: CORS governs browser cross-origin access. Non-browser clients are not restricted by it, and some browser requests can still be sent. [Source](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS).

questions.question: A browser application authenticates with automatically attached cookies. Which measures help protect state-changing endpoints against CSRF?
options: Validate an appropriate anti-CSRF token
Use `SameSite` cookie settings as part of a layered defense
Assume `HttpOnly` cookies alone prevent CSRF
Validate `Origin` or suitable fallback request-origin information
answers: Validate an appropriate anti-CSRF token
Use `SameSite` cookie settings as part of a layered defense
Validate `Origin` or suitable fallback request-origin information
questions.explanation: Browsers can attach cookies to attacker-triggered requests. `HttpOnly` restricts script access to cookies, not their automatic transmission. [Source](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html).

questions.question: A payment creation request times out after it may have succeeded. The API supports idempotency keys. What is the safest retry approach within its documented retention window?
options: Retry the same logical request with the same key and unchanged payload
Generate a fresh key to avoid a cached result
Assume timeout proves failure and issue another payment
Retry without a key because the first response was lost
questions.answer: Retry the same logical request with the same key and unchanged payload
questions.explanation: A stable key identifies one intent across attempts. A new key can represent a new operation and duplicate the payment. [Source](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests).

questions.question: Which properties should a robust idempotency-key implementation include?
options: Appropriate key scoping to the caller or tenant
Rejection of key reuse with a different request intent
Atomic coordination of concurrent requests using the same key
An unlimited guarantee even after all deduplication records expire
answers: Appropriate key scoping to the caller or tenant
Rejection of key reuse with a different request intent
Atomic coordination of concurrent requests using the same key
questions.explanation: Concurrent attempts must agree on one operation. Define payload matching, in-progress behavior, and retention limits explicitly. [Source](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/).

questions.question: A webhook receiver must acknowledge quickly and survive crashes without losing accepted work. Which sequence best meets that contract?
options: Return success, then keep the event only in memory
Validate authenticity, durably accept or identify the duplicate, acknowledge, then process asynchronously
Finish all slow downstream calls before recording the event
Acknowledge any event with a familiar-looking identifier without validation
questions.answer: Validate authenticity, durably accept or identify the duplicate, acknowledge, then process asynchronously
questions.explanation: Durable acceptance closes the crash gap between acknowledgment and processing. Retries still require duplicate handling; signatures establish event authenticity. [Source](https://docs.stripe.com/webhooks).

questions.question: A token bucket has capacity 20, currently contains 20 tokens, and refills at 5 tokens/second. Each request costs one token. For an instantaneous burst with no refill during evaluation, how many requests can it admit?
questions.explanation: Current tokens determine immediate admission; refill controls later capacity. Bucket size allows bounded bursts above the sustained rate. [Source](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/configuration/http/http_filters/local_rate_limit_filter).

questions.question: A fixed-window limiter allows 100 requests per calendar minute. With no other restrictions, how many can pass in a two-second interval straddling a minute boundary?
options: At most 100
At most 102
At most 50
Up to 200
questions.answer: Up to 200
questions.explanation: A client can consume one window’s allowance just before reset and the next immediately afterward. This is a boundary-burst weakness.

questions.question: Ten replicas each independently permit the same customer 100 requests/minute. What is the problem if the advertised limit is globally 100?
options: The customer can consume separate allowances across replicas unless enforcement is coordinated
Local counters automatically synchronize through the load balancer
The customer is necessarily limited to 10 requests/minute
TLS makes the counters globally consistent
questions.answer: The customer can consume separate allowances across replicas unless enforcement is coordinated
questions.explanation: Replica-local limits are not global quotas. Use coordinated accounting or allocated budgets with defined consistency and failure behavior. [Source](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/other_features/global_rate_limiting).

questions.question: A semaphore limiting an API client to 20 in-flight requests guarantees it sends no more than 20 requests per second.
questions.explanation: Concurrency measures simultaneous work; rate measures admissions over time. Fast completions can produce high throughput under a small concurrency limit. [Source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/rate-limiting-pattern).

questions.question: The shared rate-limit service is unavailable. Which policy decision should be made explicitly?
options: Always allow traffic because correctness is unaffected
Choose fail-open, fail-closed, or bounded local fallback based on abuse risk and availability requirements
Always retry every admission check without a deadline
Assume the advertised quota remains exact without any accounting
questions.answer: Choose fail-open, fail-closed, or bounded local fallback based on abuse risk and availability requirements
questions.explanation: There is a trade-off between enforcement and availability during failures. A fallback must document the protection it can actually preserve.

questions.question: For HTTP responses, which distinction between `Cache-Control: no-cache` (without a field-name argument) and `Cache-Control: no-store` is correct?
options: Both prohibit storing any response
`no-cache` permits unrestricted reuse while `no-store` requires validation
`no-cache` allows storage but requires validation before reuse; `no-store` forbids storage under the directive’s rules
`no-store` means store only for the current browser session
questions.answer: `no-cache` allows storage but requires validation before reuse; `no-store` forbids storage under the directive’s rules
questions.explanation: The unqualified `no-cache` response directive permits storage but requires successful validation before reuse. `no-store` forbids storage under the directive’s rules. The field-qualified form of `no-cache` has different rules and is outside this question’s scope. [Source](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html#section-5.2.2.4).

questions.question: An application cache holds personalized responses. Which safeguards are appropriate?
options: Include relevant tenant, identity, and representation dimensions in the cache design
Authorize access to cached content as well as uncached content
Use only the URL as the key regardless of user identity
Use `private` or `no-store` HTTP policies where shared caching is inappropriate
answers: Include relevant tenant, identity, and representation dimensions in the cache design
Authorize access to cached content as well as uncached content
Use `private` or `no-store` HTTP policies where shared caching is inappropriate
questions.explanation: Caching must preserve access boundaries. Application cache keys and HTTP shared-cache policies solve related but distinct problems. [Source](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html).

questions.question: A popular public cache entry expires and thousands of requests start the same expensive refresh. Which combination most directly reduces the stampede?
options: Retries without delays from every caller
Identical expiry times across every entry
Disabling all concurrency limits
Coalesce refreshes per key and vary expiry times; serve bounded stale data only if permitted
questions.answer: Coalesce refreshes per key and vary expiry times; serve bounded stale data only if permitted
questions.explanation: Coalescing refreshes for the same key prevents duplicate work for that entry. Expiry jitter spreads misses across different entries; it does not by itself solve simultaneous requests for one expired key. Serving stale data is appropriate only when the freshness contract permits it. [Source](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/caching-challenges-and-strategies/).

questions.question: A cache-aside reader loads an old value, a writer updates the source and invalidates the key, then the reader caches its old value. What does this show?
options: Invalidation alone can race with readers; version-aware fills or coordination may be needed
Cache-aside guarantees linearizable reads
The writer must have failed because invalidation prevents all stale fills
A longer TTL eliminates this race
questions.answer: Invalidation alone can race with readers; version-aware fills or coordination may be needed
questions.explanation: An in-flight stale read can repopulate an invalidated key. TTL bounds persistence but does not eliminate the consistency gap. [Source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cache-aside).

questions.question: A cached authorization decision says allow, but permission was just revoked and revocation must take effect immediately. What should the design avoid?
options: Checking current policy at the enforcement boundary
Serving stale allow decisions as an availability fallback
Invalidating permission cache entries on policy changes
Separating public content caching from authorization decisions
questions.answer: Serving stale allow decisions as an availability fallback
questions.explanation: Freshness is part of the security requirement. Availability fallbacks must not silently extend revoked access. [Source](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html).

questions.question: Which conditions belong in a safe retry policy for an external API?
options: Retry only eligible failures and operations that can be repeated safely
Use bounded attempts, backoff, and jitter
Retry permanent validation errors until a success appears
Respect applicable `Retry-After` guidance and the overall deadline
answers: Retry only eligible failures and operations that can be repeated safely
Use bounded attempts, backoff, and jitter
Respect applicable `Retry-After` guidance and the overall deadline
questions.explanation: Retries consume time and capacity. Bound them, distinguish transient failures, and preserve operation identity when side effects are possible. [Source](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/retry-backoff.html). [Jitter](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/exponential-backoff-and-jitter/).

questions.question: Three nested service layers each make at most three total attempts per incoming attempt. Every attempt reaches the next layer and all fail. How many attempts can reach the deepest dependency for one top-level request?
questions.explanation: The counts multiply: 3 × 3 × 3. Choose a deliberate retry owner or shared budget to prevent amplification.

questions.question: A request has a one-second end-to-end deadline. Its first dependency consumes 800 ms. How should the remaining dependency calls be budgeted?
options: Each receives a fresh one-second timeout
Each receives an unlimited timeout if it is idempotent
The deadline resets after every successful call
Propagate the remaining budget, reserving time for local work and response delivery
questions.answer: Propagate the remaining budget, reserving time for local work and response delivery
questions.explanation: Per-hop timeouts should fit the remaining request deadline. Resetting the full budget at every hop can exceed the caller’s bound. [Source](https://grpc.io/docs/guides/deadlines/).

questions.question: A dependency is repeatedly failing. What distinguishes a circuit breaker from a retry loop?
options: The breaker can temporarily reject calls without attempting the dependency
The breaker guarantees every rejected call will later succeed
The breaker removes the need for timeouts
The breaker duplicates every request to increase success probability
questions.answer: The breaker can temporarily reject calls without attempting the dependency
questions.explanation: A breaker stops repeated calls during sustained failure. Retries attempt recovery from selected failures; the patterns have different jobs. [Source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/circuit-breaker).

questions.question: Why does a circuit breaker typically allow only limited traffic in its half-open state?
options: To permanently reduce the dependency’s capacity
To test recovery without immediately restoring the full load
To bypass authentication while diagnosing failures
To guarantee that all prior failures are rolled back
questions.answer: To test recovery without immediately restoring the full load
questions.explanation: Controlled probes provide evidence of recovery. Their outcomes guide reopening or closing the circuit without a sudden traffic surge. [Source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/circuit-breaker).

questions.question: Slow optional analytics calls exhaust a shared connection pool and block critical checkout calls. Which pattern most directly limits this failure’s spread?
options: A larger unbounded shared queue
Identical retry policies for both dependencies
Separate bounded resource pools for critical and optional dependencies
A single global lock around both call types
questions.answer: Separate bounded resource pools for critical and optional dependencies
questions.explanation: Bulkheads partition resources so one dependency cannot consume every connection or worker needed by unrelated operations. [Source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/bulkhead).

questions.question: An asynchronous API accepts jobs faster than workers can process them for hours. Which design best prevents unbounded resource growth?
options: Return success for every request and store the backlog only in RAM
Add retries to every queued item regardless of failure
Increase the queue limit indefinitely
Bound admitted work, monitor queue age, and reject or defer excess load according to the contract
questions.answer: Bound admitted work, monitor queue age, and reject or defer excess load according to the contract
questions.explanation: Queues absorb bursts, not unlimited sustained overload. Admission control and capacity planning must account for backlog size and processing delay. [Source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/queue-based-load-leveling).

questions.question: A dashboard aggregates required account data and optional recommendations. Recommendations time out. If the product permits degraded responses, what is the best API behavior?
options: Return the account data with an explicit indication that recommendations are unavailable
Fabricate recommendations and report a fully successful result
Always wait indefinitely because the account call succeeded
Retry the entire aggregate operation without a budget
questions.answer: Return the account data with an explicit indication that recommendations are unavailable
questions.explanation: Define partial-result semantics so clients can distinguish unavailable data from an empty result. Bound optional work and expose degradation. [Source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/gateway-aggregation).
